summary: Queue depth grew for 27 minutes without an increase in arrival rate, while consumer throughput fell ~40%, indicating a consumer-side slowdown rather than a load surge. Two candidate causes were introduced in the preceding hour (a consumer-library upgrade and a database index rebuild), and the logs contain signals consistent with each (lock-wait messages and deserialization warnings). The available evidence cannot attribute the stall to either change individually: the only recovery observation reverted both changes together, no single-revert run exists, telemetry does not separate database-wait time from deserialization-retry time, and no traces were retained. The supported conclusion is that one or both of the two changes caused the throughput loss, with the split between them unresolved.

claims.text: The backlog growth was caused by reduced consumer processing capacity, not by increased incoming load.
Consumer throughput dropped roughly 40% over the same 27-minute window in which queue depth rose.
Two changes in the preceding hour are temporally eligible as causes: a consumer-library upgrade and a database index rebuild.
At least one of the two changes caused the throughput loss, since reverting both restored normal throughput.
The evidence does not determine whether the library upgrade, the index rebuild, or both together produced the slowdown.
Increased lock-wait messages are consistent with database-side contention, which the index rebuild could plausibly produce.
Increased deserialization warnings are consistent with a message-decoding regression, which the consumer-library upgrade could plausibly produce.
Both log signals rose together, so neither signal on its own discriminates between the two candidate causes.
The instrumentation in place cannot apportion consumer processing time between database waiting and deserialization retries.
No retained traces exist for the incident window, so after-the-fact per-request attribution is not possible from stored data.
The joint revert is a confounded experiment: its outcome is equally consistent with a single-cause and a two-cause explanation.
The evidence does not establish that the observed log warnings, rather than some unmeasured effect of the changes, are the mechanism of the slowdown.

uncertainties.text: Whether the library upgrade, the index rebuild, or their combination caused the throughput loss.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: A run in which exactly one change is reverted (or reapplied) while the other is held fixed, with throughput measured.

uncertainties.text: How consumer processing time divided between database waiting and deserialization retries.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: Instrumentation that times database calls and deserialization paths separately within the consumer.

uncertainties.text: Whether the elevated lock-wait and deserialization messages were causally on the critical path or incidental correlates.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: Per-message traces or profiles linking the warning events to the slow processing intervals.

uncertainties.text: Whether the two effects were additive, interacting, or whether one was entirely a side effect of the other.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: A factorial test covering both single-change conditions plus the combined condition.

uncertainties.text: Whether an unlisted third factor coincident with the change window contributed.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: A complete change and environment log for the incident window beyond the two changes named.

uncertainties.text: Whether the index rebuild's effect was transient (only during rebuild) or persistent after completion.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: Rebuild start and completion timestamps compared against the throughput curve.

uncertainties.text: Whether deserialization warnings represented failed-and-retried work or logged-but-harmless conditions.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: Retry and failure counters for the deserialization path, and the warning text semantics.

uncertainties.text: Whether recovery after the joint revert was caused by the revert or by independent resolution over time.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: A control observation of throughput held under the changed configuration past the revert time.

actions.text: Run a single-variable test: reapply one change alone in a controlled environment and measure throughput, then repeat for the other.
Add separate timers for database call wait and deserialization/retry work in the consumer so the two costs can be apportioned.
Enable and retain trace sampling covering the consumer path so a future incident window has per-request evidence.
Reconstruct an exact change timeline, including index-rebuild start and finish times, and align it to the throughput and queue-depth curves.
Instrument deserialization outcomes as counters (attempts, failures, retries) rather than warning text only.
Adopt a change policy that separates independent changes in time so recovery observations are not confounded.

counterfactuals.text: If only the library upgrade had been reverted and throughput had recovered, the upgrade would be identified as sufficient cause and the index rebuild demoted.
If only the index rebuild had been reverted and throughput had recovered, the rebuild would be identified as sufficient cause.
If either single revert had left throughput depressed but both reverts restored it, a joint or interacting cause would be indicated.
If telemetry had separated database wait from deserialization retry time, the dominant cost centre would be visible without any revert experiment.
If arrival rate had risen instead of staying normal, the backlog could have been explained by load rather than by consumer degradation.
If only one of the two log signals had increased, that signal would have pointed to its corresponding change, though still without proof of mechanism.
